content: Chenopodium is a genus comprising approximately 150 species of herbaceous flowering plants, either annual or perennial, commonly referred to as goosefoots. These plants are distributed globally and belong to the family Amaranthaceae under the APG II classification system. Historically, they were classified under the family Chenopodiaceae, but this classification rendered the remaining Amaranthaceae polyphyletic. Within the Amaranthaceae family, Chenopodium is the representative genus of the subfamily Chenopodioideae. The genus Dysphania is closely related to Chenopodium and includes species that were previously classified under Chenopodium, such as epazote (Dysphania ambrosioides). In Australia, larger species of Chenopodium are colloquially referred to as bluebushes. The town of Chualar in California derives its name from a Native American term for a goosefoot species abundant in the area, likely the California goosefoot (Chenopodium californicum). Several species within the Chenopodium genus are utilized as food crops, either as leafy vegetables or pseudocereals. These plants are often consumed in a manner similar to spinach (Spinacia oleracea) and are known as quelite in Mexico. Notable examples include white goosefoot (Chenopodium album), Good King Henry (Chenopodium bonus-henricus), strawberry blite (Chenopodium capitatum), leafy goosefoot (Chenopodium foliosum), kañiwa (Chenopodium pallidicaule), and quinoa (Chenopodium quinoa). On the Greek island of Crete, the tender shoots and leaves of a species referred to as krouvida (κρουβίδα) or psarovlito (ψαρόβλητο) are consumed after boiling or steaming. Archaeological studies, such as those by Kristen Gremillion, indicate that goosefoots have been used as food since at least 4000 BC. For instance, pitseed goosefoot (Chenopodium berlandieri) was a staple crop in the Native American Eastern Agricultural Complex, while white goosefoot was utilized by the Ertebølle culture in Europe. In modern times, there is growing interest in the seeds of goosefoot species, particularly for their suitability in gluten-free diets. Quinoa oil, derived from the seeds of Chenopodium quinoa, is of higher quality than corn oil and shares similar properties. Oil of chenopodium, however, is extracted from the seeds of epazote, which is no longer classified within this genus. Historically, the small, hard seeds of goosefoot plants were used to produce shagreen leather. Chenopodium album has also served as a model organism for molecular biological studies of chlorophyllase. The pollen of goosefoot species, particularly Chenopodium album, is a common allergen and a frequent cause of hay fever. Additionally, the seeds of some species can remain viable in the soil seed bank for years, contributing to their persistence as weeds. Certain species have become invasive, forming dense thickets that provide shelter for small animals. The foliage of goosefoot plants serves as a food source for the caterpillars of specific Lepidoptera species, while the seeds are consumed by various bird species, such as the yellowhammer (Emberiza citrinella) in Europe and the white-winged fairy-wren (Malurus leucopterus) in Australia. Goosefoot plants are susceptible to several pathogens, including positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses such as the apple stem grooving virus, sowbane mosaic virus, and tobacco necrosis virus.
